CHAPTER XII.
A NIGHT WITH DURDLES


When Mr. Sapsea has nothing better to do, towards evening, and finds
the contemplation of his own profundity becoming a little monotonous in
spite of the vastness of the subject, he often takes an airing in the
Cathedral Close and thereabout. He likes to pass the churchyard with a
swelling air of proprietorship, and to encourage in his breast a sort
of benignant-landlord feeling, in that he has been bountiful towards
that meritorious tenant, Mrs. Sapsea, and has publicly given her a
prize. He likes to see a stray face or two looking in through the
railings, and perhaps reading his inscription. Should he meet a
stranger coming from the churchyard with a quick step, he is morally
convinced that the stranger is “with a blush retiring,” as monumentally
directed.

Mr. Sapsea’s importance has received enhancement, for he has become
Mayor of Cloisterham. Without mayors, and many of them, it cannot be
disputed that the whole framework of society—Mr. Sapsea is confident
that he invented that forcible figure—would fall to pieces. Mayors have
been knighted for “going up” with addresses: explosive machines
intrepidly discharging shot and shell into the English Grammar. Mr.
Sapsea may “go up” with an address. Rise, Sir Thomas Sapsea! Of such is
the salt of the earth.

Mr. Sapsea has improved the acquaintance of Mr. Jasper, since their
first meeting to partake of port, epitaph, backgammon, beef, and salad.
Mr. Sapsea has been received at the gatehouse with kindred hospitality;
and on that occasion Mr. Jasper seated himself at the piano, and sang
to him, tickling his ears—figuratively—long enough to present a
considerable area for tickling. What Mr. Sapsea likes in that young man
is, that he is always ready to profit by the wisdom of his elders, and
that he is sound, sir, at the core. In proof of which, he sang to Mr.
Sapsea that evening, no kickshaw ditties, favourites with national
enemies, but gave him the genuine George the Third home-brewed;
exhorting him (as “my brave boys”) to reduce to a smashed condition all
other islands but this island, and all continents, peninsulas,
isthmuses, promontories, and other geographical forms of land soever,
besides sweeping the seas in all directions. In short, he rendered it
pretty clear that Providence made a distinct mistake in originating so
small a nation of hearts of oak, and so many other verminous peoples.

Mr. Sapsea, walking slowly this moist evening near the churchyard with
his hands behind him, on the look-out for a blushing and retiring
stranger, turns a corner, and comes instead into the goodly presence of
the Dean, conversing with the Verger and Mr. Jasper. Mr. Sapsea makes
his obeisance, and is instantly stricken far more ecclesiastical than
any Archbishop of York or Canterbury.

“You are evidently going to write a book about us, Mr. Jasper,” quoth
the Dean; “to write a book about us. Well! We are very ancient, and we
ought to make a good book. We are not so richly endowed in possessions
as in age; but perhaps you will put _that_ in your book, among other
things, and call attention to our wrongs.”

Mr. Tope, as in duty bound, is greatly entertained by this.

“I really have no intention at all, sir,” replies Jasper, “of turning
author or archæologist. It is but a whim of mine. And even for my whim,
Mr. Sapsea here is more accountable than I am.”

“How so, Mr. Mayor?” says the Dean, with a nod of good-natured
recognition of his Fetch. “How is that, Mr. Mayor?”

“I am not aware,” Mr. Sapsea remarks, looking about him for
information, “to what the Very Reverend the Dean does me the honour of
referring.” And then falls to studying his original in minute points of
detail.

“Durdles,” Mr. Tope hints.

“Ay!” the Dean echoes; “Durdles, Durdles!”

“The truth is, sir,” explains Jasper, “that my curiosity in the man was
first really stimulated by Mr. Sapsea. Mr. Sapsea’s knowledge of
mankind and power of drawing out whatever is recluse or odd around him,
first led to my bestowing a second thought upon the man: though of
course I had met him constantly about. You would not be surprised by
this, Mr. Dean, if you had seen Mr. Sapsea deal with him in his own
parlour, as I did.”

“O!” cries Sapsea, picking up the ball thrown to him with ineffable
complacency and pomposity; “yes, yes. The Very Reverend the Dean refers
to that? Yes. I happened to bring Durdles and Mr. Jasper together. I
regard Durdles as a Character.”

“A character, Mr. Sapsea, that with a few skilful touches you turn
inside out,” says Jasper.

“Nay, not quite that,” returns the lumbering auctioneer. “I may have a
little influence over him, perhaps; and a little insight into his
character, perhaps. The Very Reverend the Dean will please to bear in
mind that I have seen the world.” Here Mr. Sapsea gets a little behind
the Dean, to inspect his coat-buttons.

“Well!” says the Dean, looking about him to see what has become of his
copyist: “I hope, Mr. Mayor, you will use your study and knowledge of
Durdles to the good purpose of exhorting him not to break our worthy
and respected Choir-Master’s neck; we cannot afford it; his head and
voice are much too valuable to us.”

Mr. Tope is again highly entertained, and, having fallen into
respectful convulsions of laughter, subsides into a deferential murmur,
importing that surely any gentleman would deem it a pleasure and an
honour to have his neck broken, in return for such a compliment from
such a source.

“I will take it upon myself, sir,” observes Sapsea loftily, “to answer
for Mr. Jasper’s neck. I will tell Durdles to be careful of it. He will
mind what _I_ say. How is it at present endangered?” he inquires,
looking about him with magnificent patronage.

“Only by my making a moonlight expedition with Durdles among the tombs,
vaults, towers, and ruins,” returns Jasper. “You remember suggesting,
when you brought us together, that, as a lover of the picturesque, it
might be worth my while?”

“I remember!” replies the auctioneer. And the solemn idiot really
believes that he does remember.

“Profiting by your hint,” pursues Jasper, “I have had some day-rambles
with the extraordinary old fellow, and we are to make a moonlight
hole-and-corner exploration to-night.”

“And here he is,” says the Dean.

Durdles with his dinner-bundle in his hand, is indeed beheld slouching
towards them. Slouching nearer, and perceiving the Dean, he pulls off
his hat, and is slouching away with it under his arm, when Mr. Sapsea
stops him.

“Mind you take care of my friend,” is the injunction Mr. Sapsea lays
upon him.

“What friend o’ yourn is dead?” asks Durdles. “No orders has come in
for any friend o’ yourn.”

“I mean my live friend there.”

“O! him?” says Durdles. “He can take care of himself, can Mister
Jarsper.”

“But do you take care of him too,” says Sapsea.

Whom Durdles (there being command in his tone) surlily surveys from
head to foot.

“With submission to his Reverence the Dean, if you’ll mind what
concerns you, Mr. Sapsea, Durdles he’ll mind what concerns him.”

“You’re out of temper,” says Mr. Sapsea, winking to the company to
observe how smoothly he will manage him. “My friend concerns me, and
Mr. Jasper is my friend. And you are my friend.”

“Don’t you get into a bad habit of boasting,” retorts Durdles, with a
grave cautionary nod. “It’ll grow upon you.”

[Illustration: Durdles cautions Mr. Sapsea against boasting]


“You are out of temper,” says Sapsea again; reddening, but again
sinking to the company.

“I own to it,” returns Durdles; “I don’t like liberties.”

Mr. Sapsea winks a third wink to the company, as who should say: “I
think you will agree with me that I have settled _his_ business;” and
stalks out of the controversy.

Durdles then gives the Dean a good evening, and adding, as he puts his
hat on, “You’ll find me at home, Mister Jarsper, as agreed, when you
want me; I’m a-going home to clean myself,” soon slouches out of sight.
This going home to clean himself is one of the man’s incomprehensible
compromises with inexorable facts; he, and his hat, and his boots, and
his clothes, never showing any trace of cleaning, but being uniformly
in one condition of dust and grit.

The lamplighter now dotting the quiet Close with specks of light, and
running at a great rate up and down his little ladder with that
object—his little ladder under the sacred shadow of whose inconvenience
generations had grown up, and which all Cloisterham would have stood
aghast at the idea of abolishing—the Dean withdraws to his dinner, Mr.
Tope to his tea, and Mr. Jasper to his piano. There, with no light but
that of the fire, he sits chanting choir-music in a low and beautiful
voice, for two or three hours; in short, until it has been for some
time dark, and the moon is about to rise.

Then he closes his piano softly, softly changes his coat for a
pea-jacket, with a goodly wicker-cased bottle in its largest pocket,
and putting on a low-crowned, flap-brimmed hat, goes softly out. Why
does he move so softly to-night? No outward reason is apparent for it.
Can there be any sympathetic reason crouching darkly within him?

Repairing to Durdles’s unfinished house, or hole in the city wall, and
seeing a light within it, he softly picks his course among the
gravestones, monuments, and stony lumber of the yard, already touched
here and there, sidewise, by the rising moon. The two journeymen have
left their two great saws sticking in their blocks of stone; and two
skeleton journeymen out of the Dance of Death might be grinning in the
shadow of their sheltering sentry-boxes, about to slash away at cutting
out the gravestones of the next two people destined to die in
Cloisterham. Likely enough, the two think little of that now, being
alive, and perhaps merry. Curious, to make a guess at the two;—or say
one of the two!

“Ho! Durdles!”

The light moves, and he appears with it at the door. He would seem to
have been “cleaning himself” with the aid of a bottle, jug, and
tumbler; for no other cleansing instruments are visible in the bare
brick room with rafters overhead and no plastered ceiling, into which
he shows his visitor.

“Are you ready?”

“I am ready, Mister Jarsper. Let the old ’uns come out if they dare,
when we go among their tombs. My spirit is ready for ’em.”

“Do you mean animal spirits, or ardent?”

“The one’s the t’other,” answers Durdles, “and I mean ’em both.”

He takes a lantern from a hook, puts a match or two in his pocket
wherewith to light it, should there be need; and they go out together,
dinner-bundle and all.

Surely an unaccountable sort of expedition! That Durdles himself, who
is always prowling among old graves, and ruins, like a Ghoul—that he
should be stealing forth to climb, and dive, and wander without an
object, is nothing extraordinary; but that the Choir-Master or any one
else should hold it worth his while to be with him, and to study
moonlight effects in such company is another affair. Surely an
unaccountable sort of expedition, therefore!

“’Ware that there mound by the yard-gate, Mister Jarsper.”

“I see it. What is it?”

“Lime.”

Mr. Jasper stops, and waits for him to come up, for he lags behind.
“What you call quick-lime?”

“Ay!” says Durdles; “quick enough to eat your boots. With a little
handy stirring, quick enough to eat your bones.”

They go on, presently passing the red windows of the Travellers’
Twopenny, and emerging into the clear moonlight of the Monks’ Vineyard.
This crossed, they come to Minor Canon Corner: of which the greater
part lies in shadow until the moon shall rise higher in the sky.

The sound of a closing house-door strikes their ears, and two men come
out. These are Mr. Crisparkle and Neville. Jasper, with a strange and
sudden smile upon his face, lays the palm of his hand upon the breast
of Durdles, stopping him where he stands.

At that end of Minor Canon Corner the shadow is profound in the
existing state of the light: at that end, too, there is a piece of old
dwarf wall, breast high, the only remaining boundary of what was once a
garden, but is now the thoroughfare. Jasper and Durdles would have
turned this wall in another instant; but, stopping so short, stand
behind it.

“Those two are only sauntering,” Jasper whispers; “they will go out
into the moonlight soon. Let us keep quiet here, or they will detain
us, or want to join us, or what not.”

Durdles nods assent, and falls to munching some fragments from his
bundle. Jasper folds his arms upon the top of the wall, and, with his
chin resting on them, watches. He takes no note whatever of the Minor
Canon, but watches Neville, as though his eye were at the trigger of a
loaded rifle, and he had covered him, and were going to fire. A sense
of destructive power is so expressed in his face, that even Durdles
pauses in his munching, and looks at him, with an unmunched something
in his cheek.

Meanwhile Mr. Crisparkle and Neville walk to and fro, quietly talking
together. What they say, cannot be heard consecutively; but Mr. Jasper
has already distinguished his own name more than once.

“This is the first day of the week,” Mr. Crisparkle can be distinctly
heard to observe, as they turn back; “and the last day of the week is
Christmas Eve.”

“You may be certain of me, sir.”

The echoes were favourable at those points, but as the two approach,
the sound of their talking becomes confused again. The word
“confidence,” shattered by the echoes, but still capable of being
pieced together, is uttered by Mr. Crisparkle. As they draw still
nearer, this fragment of a reply is heard: “Not deserved yet, but shall
be, sir.” As they turn away again, Jasper again hears his own name, in
connection with the words from Mr. Crisparkle: “Remember that I said I
answered for you confidently.” Then the sound of their talk becomes
confused again; they halting for a little while, and some earnest
action on the part of Neville succeeding. When they move once more, Mr.
Crisparkle is seen to look up at the sky, and to point before him. They
then slowly disappear; passing out into the moonlight at the opposite
end of the Corner.

It is not until they are gone, that Mr. Jasper moves. But then he turns
to Durdles, and bursts into a fit of laughter. Durdles, who still has
that suspended something in his cheek, and who sees nothing to laugh
at, stares at him until Mr. Jasper lays his face down on his arms to
have his laugh out. Then Durdles bolts the something, as if desperately
resigning himself to indigestion.

Among those secluded nooks there is very little stir or movement after
dark. There is little enough in the high tide of the day, but there is
next to none at night. Besides that the cheerfully frequented High
Street lies nearly parallel to the spot (the old Cathedral rising
between the two), and is the natural channel in which the Cloisterham
traffic flows, a certain awful hush pervades the ancient pile, the
cloisters, and the churchyard, after dark, which not many people care
to encounter. Ask the first hundred citizens of Cloisterham, met at
random in the streets at noon, if they believed in Ghosts, they would
tell you no; but put them to choose at night between these eerie
Precincts and the thoroughfare of shops, and you would find that
ninety-nine declared for the longer round and the more frequented way.
The cause of this is not to be found in any local superstition that
attaches to the Precincts—albeit a mysterious lady, with a child in her
arms and a rope dangling from her neck, has been seen flitting about
there by sundry witnesses as intangible as herself—but it is to be
sought in the innate shrinking of dust with the breath of life in it
from dust out of which the breath of life has passed; also, in the
widely diffused, and almost as widely unacknowledged, reflection: “If
the dead do, under any circumstances, become visible to the living,
these are such likely surroundings for the purpose that I, the living,
will get out of them as soon as I can.” Hence, when Mr. Jasper and
Durdles pause to glance around them, before descending into the crypt
by a small side door, of which the latter has a key, the whole expanse
of moonlight in their view is utterly deserted. One might fancy that
the tide of life was stemmed by Mr. Jasper’s own gatehouse. The murmur
of the tide is heard beyond; but no wave passes the archway, over which
his lamp burns red behind his curtain, as if the building were a
Lighthouse.

They enter, locking themselves in, descend the rugged steps, and are
down in the Crypt. The lantern is not wanted, for the moonlight strikes
in at the groined windows, bare of glass, the broken frames for which
cast patterns on the ground. The heavy pillars which support the roof
engender masses of black shade, but between them there are lanes of
light. Up and down these lanes they walk, Durdles discoursing of the
“old uns” he yet counts on disinterring, and slapping a wall, in which
he considers “a whole family on ’em” to be stoned and earthed up, just
as if he were a familiar friend of the family. The taciturnity of
Durdles is for the time overcome by Mr. Jasper’s wicker bottle, which
circulates freely;—in the sense, that is to say, that its contents
enter freely into Mr. Durdles’s circulation, while Mr. Jasper only
rinses his mouth once, and casts forth the rinsing.

They are to ascend the great Tower. On the steps by which they rise to
the Cathedral, Durdles pauses for new store of breath. The steps are
very dark, but out of the darkness they can see the lanes of light they
have traversed. Durdles seats himself upon a step. Mr. Jasper seats
himself upon another. The odour from the wicker bottle (which has
somehow passed into Durdles’s keeping) soon intimates that the cork has
been taken out; but this is not ascertainable through the sense of
sight, since neither can descry the other. And yet, in talking, they
turn to one another, as though their faces could commune together.

“This is good stuff, Mister Jarsper!”

“It is very good stuff, I hope.—I bought it on purpose.”

“They don’t show, you see, the old uns don’t, Mister Jarsper!”

“It would be a more confused world than it is, if they could.”

“Well, it _would_ lead towards a mixing of things,” Durdles acquiesces:
pausing on the remark, as if the idea of ghosts had not previously
presented itself to him in a merely inconvenient light, domestically or
chronologically. “But do you think there may be Ghosts of other things,
though not of men and women?”

“What things? Flower-beds and watering-pots? Horses and harness?”

“No. Sounds.”

“What sounds?”

“Cries.”

“What cries do you mean? Chairs to mend?”

“No. I mean screeches. Now I’ll tell you, Mr. Jarsper. Wait a bit till
I put the bottle right.” Here the cork is evidently taken out again,
and replaced again. “There! _Now_ it’s right! This time last year, only
a few days later, I happened to have been doing what was correct by the
season, in the way of giving it the welcome it had a right to expect,
when them town-boys set on me at their worst. At length I gave ’em the
slip, and turned in here. And here I fell asleep. And what woke me? The
ghost of a cry. The ghost of one terrific shriek, which shriek was
followed by the ghost of the howl of a dog: a long, dismal, woeful
howl, such as a dog gives when a person’s dead. That was _my_ last
Christmas Eve.”

“What do you mean?” is the very abrupt, and, one might say, fierce
retort.

“I mean that I made inquiries everywhere about, and, that no living
ears but mine heard either that cry or that howl. So I say they was
both ghosts; though why they came to me, I’ve never made out.”

“I thought you were another kind of man,” says Jasper, scornfully.

“So I thought myself,” answers Durdles with his usual composure; “and
yet I was picked out for it.”

Jasper had risen suddenly, when he asked him what he meant, and he now
says, “Come; we shall freeze here; lead the way.”

Durdles complies, not over-steadily; opens the door at the top of the
steps with the key he has already used; and so emerges on the Cathedral
level, in a passage at the side of the chancel. Here, the moonlight is
so very bright again that the colours of the nearest stained-glass
window are thrown upon their faces. The appearance of the unconscious
Durdles, holding the door open for his companion to follow, as if from
the grave, is ghastly enough, with a purple hand across his face, and a
yellow splash upon his brow; but he bears the close scrutiny of his
companion in an insensible way, although it is prolonged while the
latter fumbles among his pockets for a key confided to him that will
open an iron gate, so to enable them to pass to the staircase of the
great tower.

“That and the bottle are enough for you to carry,” he says, giving it
to Durdles; “hand your bundle to me; I am younger and longer-winded
than you.” Durdles hesitates for a moment between bundle and bottle;
but gives the preference to the bottle as being by far the better
company, and consigns the dry weight to his fellow-explorer.

Then they go up the winding staircase of the great tower, toilsomely,
turning and turning, and lowering their heads to avoid the stairs
above, or the rough stone pivot around which they twist. Durdles has
lighted his lantern, by drawing from the cold, hard wall a spark of
that mysterious fire which lurks in everything, and, guided by this
speck, they clamber up among the cobwebs and the dust. Their way lies
through strange places. Twice or thrice they emerge into level,
low-arched galleries, whence they can look down into the moonlit nave;
and where Durdles, waving his lantern, waves the dim angels’ heads upon
the corbels of the roof, seeming to watch their progress. Anon they
turn into narrower and steeper staircases, and the night-air begins to
blow upon them, and the chirp of some startled jackdaw or frightened
rook precedes the heavy beating of wings in a confined space, and the
beating down of dust and straws upon their heads. At last, leaving
their light behind a stair—for it blows fresh up here—they look down on
Cloisterham, fair to see in the moonlight: its ruined habitations and
sanctuaries of the dead, at the tower’s base: its moss-softened
red-tiled roofs and red-brick houses of the living, clustered beyond:
its river winding down from the mist on the horizon, as though that
were its source, and already heaving with a restless knowledge of its
approach towards the sea.

Once again, an unaccountable expedition this! Jasper (always moving
softly with no visible reason) contemplates the scene, and especially
that stillest part of it which the Cathedral overshadows. But he
contemplates Durdles quite as curiously, and Durdles is by times
conscious of his watchful eyes.

Only by times, because Durdles is growing drowsy. As aëronauts lighten
the load they carry, when they wish to rise, similarly Durdles has
lightened the wicker bottle in coming up. Snatches of sleep surprise
him on his legs, and stop him in his talk. A mild fit of calenture
seizes him, in which he deems that the ground so far below, is on a
level with the tower, and would as lief walk off the tower into the air
as not. Such is his state when they begin to come down. And as
aëronauts make themselves heavier when they wish to descend, similarly
Durdles charges himself with more liquid from the wicker bottle, that
he may come down the better.

The iron gate attained and locked—but not before Durdles has tumbled
twice, and cut an eyebrow open once—they descend into the crypt again,
with the intent of issuing forth as they entered. But, while returning
among those lanes of light, Durdles becomes so very uncertain, both of
foot and speech, that he half drops, half throws himself down, by one
of the heavy pillars, scarcely less heavy than itself, and indistinctly
appeals to his companion for forty winks of a second each.

“If you will have it so, or must have it so,” replies Jasper, “I’ll not
leave you here. Take them, while I walk to and fro.”

Durdles is asleep at once; and in his sleep he dreams a dream.

It is not much of a dream, considering the vast extent of the domains
of dreamland, and their wonderful productions; it is only remarkable
for being unusually restless and unusually real. He dreams of lying
there, asleep, and yet counting his companion’s footsteps as he walks
to and fro. He dreams that the footsteps die away into distance of time
and of space, and that something touches him, and that something falls
from his hand. Then something clinks and gropes about, and he dreams
that he is alone for so long a time, that the lanes of light take new
directions as the moon advances in her course. From succeeding
unconsciousness he passes into a dream of slow uneasiness from cold;
and painfully awakes to a perception of the lanes of light—really
changed, much as he had dreamed—and Jasper walking among them, beating
his hands and feet.

“Holloa!” Durdles cries out, unmeaningly alarmed.

“Awake at last?” says Jasper, coming up to him. “Do you know that your
forties have stretched into thousands?”

“No.”

“They have though.”

“What’s the time?”

“Hark! The bells are going in the Tower!”

They strike four quarters, and then the great bell strikes.

“Two!” cries Durdles, scrambling up; “why didn’t you try to wake me,
Mister Jarsper?”

“I did. I might as well have tried to wake the dead—your own family of
dead, up in the corner there.”

“Did you touch me?”

“Touch you! Yes. Shook you.”

As Durdles recalls that touching something in his dream, he looks down
on the pavement, and sees the key of the crypt door lying close to
where he himself lay.

“I dropped you, did I?” he says, picking it up, and recalling that part
of his dream. As he gathers himself up again into an upright position,
or into a position as nearly upright as he ever maintains, he is again
conscious of being watched by his companion.

“Well?” says Jasper, smiling, “are you quite ready? Pray don’t hurry.”

“Let me get my bundle right, Mister Jarsper, and I’m with you.” As he
ties it afresh, he is once more conscious that he is very narrowly
observed.

“What do you suspect me of, Mister Jarsper?” he asks, with drunken
displeasure. “Let them as has any suspicions of Durdles name ’em.”

“I’ve no suspicions of you, my good Mr. Durdles; but I have suspicions
that my bottle was filled with something stiffer than either of us
supposed. And I also have suspicions,” Jasper adds, taking it from the
pavement and turning it bottom upwards, “that it’s empty.”

Durdles condescends to laugh at this. Continuing to chuckle when his
laugh is over, as though remonstrant with himself on his drinking
powers, he rolls to the door and unlocks it. They both pass out, and
Durdles relocks it, and pockets his key.

“A thousand thanks for a curious and interesting night,” says Jasper,
giving him his hand; “you can make your own way home?”

“I should think so!” answers Durdles. “If you was to offer Durdles the
affront to show him his way home, he wouldn’t go home.

Durdles wouldn’t go home till morning;
And _then_ Durdles wouldn’t go home,


Durdles wouldn’t.” This with the utmost defiance.

“Good-night, then.”

“Good-night, Mister Jarsper.”

Each is turning his own way, when a sharp whistle rends the silence,
and the jargon is yelped out:

Widdy widdy wen!
I—ket—ches—Im—out—ar—ter—ten.
Widdy widdy wy!
Then—E—don’t—go—then—I—shy—
Widdy Widdy Wake-cock warning!”


Instantly afterwards, a rapid fire of stones rattles at the Cathedral
wall, and the hideous small boy is beheld opposite, dancing in the
moonlight.

“What! Is that baby-devil on the watch there!” cries Jasper in a fury:
so quickly roused, and so violent, that he seems an older devil
himself. “I shall shed the blood of that impish wretch! I know I shall
do it!” Regardless of the fire, though it hits him more than once, he
rushes at Deputy, collars him, and tries to bring him across. But
Deputy is not to be so easily brought across. With a diabolical insight
into the strongest part of his position, he is no sooner taken by the
throat than he curls up his legs, forces his assailant to hang him, as
it were, and gurgles in his throat, and screws his body, and twists, as
already undergoing the first agonies of strangulation. There is nothing
for it but to drop him. He instantly gets himself together, backs over
to Durdles, and cries to his assailant, gnashing the great gap in front
of his mouth with rage and malice:

“I’ll blind yer, s’elp me! I’ll stone yer eyes out, s’elp me! If I
don’t have yer eyesight, bellows me!” At the same time dodging behind
Durdles, and snarling at Jasper, now from this side of him, and now
from that: prepared, if pounced upon, to dart away in all manner of
curvilinear directions, and, if run down after all, to grovel in the
dust, and cry: “Now, hit me when I’m down! Do it!”

“Don’t hurt the boy, Mister Jarsper,” urges Durdles, shielding him.
“Recollect yourself.”

When Mr. Sapsea had exhausted, for the day, the pleasure of admiring Mr. Sapsea, he took to the Close as to a parlour that belonged to him by right of self-importance. The air was damp enough to lay a cold hand on the railings of the churchyard; the leaves along the path held that wet, herbal smell that rises when earth has been turned and then remembered by rain. He went swelling past the graves with the proprietary gait of a landlord inspecting tenancies, pausing—if chance offered—to imagine some stranger reading his inscription and retreating, appropriately abashed, in obedience to the stone.

His consequence had lately been spiced and puffed up by office: he was Mayor now. Cloisterham, he considered, was a kind of great household that could not possibly keep its accounts, its dignity, its very joints and bones, without a Mayor to bind it together like good gravy. A Mayor might even “go up” with an address; and if English Grammar suffered a few pellets of shot and shell in the discharge, why, Grammar must bear what it could for the commonweal. Rise, Sir Thomas Sapsea—so ran his private, nutritious fancy.

He had also improved his acquaintance with Mr. Jasper, the Cathedral’s Choir-Master. Mr. Sapsea enjoyed the gatehouse for its solid comfort—port, beef, salad, backgammon, and an epitaph or two like pepper thrown over all—and he enjoyed Jasper’s deference more. Jasper would sit down at the piano after dinner and sing until the very air seemed stroked and persuaded; not with the modern, foreign frippery that Mr. Sapsea suspected of treason, but with stout old songs that marched in time like drilled men, and made the room ring as if it had been built expressly to echo national virtue. Jasper’s voice, in those moments, was a kind of domestic hearth: it warmed; it soothed; it made Mr. Sapsea feel that Providence had taken pains with English throats.

This moist evening, as the lamplighter began to seed the Close with small, steady flames—climbing and dropping his little ladder at a practised hurry, that ladder which had been part of the town’s childhood and would have been defended like a family relic—Mr. Sapsea rounded a corner by the churchyard expecting perhaps his usual phantom stranger. Instead he encountered the Dean, talking with the Verger, Mr. Tope, and with Jasper.

Mr. Sapsea bowed at once into a pitch of ecclesiastical humility that would have done credit to an Archbishop, and the Dean—whose humour was as old as the stones but not as heavy—was saying to Jasper:

“You are evidently going to write a book about us, Mr. Jasper; to write a book about us. We are very ancient, and we ought to make a good book. We are not so richly endowed in possessions as in age; but perhaps you will put that in your book, among other things, and call attention to our wrongs.”

Mr. Tope, dutifully entertained, showed his teeth in the proper reverent measure.

“I really have no intention at all, sir,” Jasper answered, “of turning author or archaeologist. It is but a whim of mine. And even for my whim, Mr. Sapsea here is more accountable than I am.”

“How so, Mr. Mayor?” asked the Dean, with a nod that acknowledged Cloisterham’s Fetch. “How is that, Mr. Mayor?”

“I am not aware,” Mr. Sapsea began, looking about him as if the answer might be hanging somewhere on the weather, “to what the Very Reverend the Dean does me the honour of referring.” And then, as if to recover himself by studying authority, he fell to examining the Dean’s person with minute attention.

“Durdles,” hinted Mr. Tope.

“Ay! Durdles,” echoed the Dean, pleased to be reminded.

“The truth is, sir,” Jasper explained, “that my curiosity in the man was first really stimulated by Mr. Sapsea. Mr. Sapsea’s knowledge of mankind and power of drawing out whatever is recluse or odd around him, first led to my bestowing a second thought upon the man—though of course I had met him constantly about. You would not be surprised by this, Mr. Dean, if you had seen Mr. Sapsea deal with him in his own parlour, as I did.”

Mr. Sapsea accepted the compliment as a man accepts a dish he thinks has been prepared in his honour: slowly, with relish, and with a look around to see who notices his appetite.

“O! yes, yes. The Very Reverend the Dean refers to that? Yes. I happened to bring Durdles and Mr. Jasper together. I regard Durdles as a Character.”

“A character,” said Jasper, “that with a few skilful touches you turn inside out.”

“Nay, not quite that,” returned Mr. Sapsea, lumbering into modesty as into a too-tight coat. “I may have a little influence over him, perhaps; and a little insight into his character, perhaps. The Very Reverend the Dean will please to bear in mind that I have seen the world.” He edged a little behind the Dean, as if to inspect the Dean’s coat-buttons and so, by proxy, inspect history itself.

“Well!” said the Dean, glancing round for his verger as though he had mislaid him in his own joke, “I hope, Mr. Mayor, you will use your study and knowledge of Durdles to the good purpose of exhorting him not to break our worthy and respected Choir-Master’s neck; we cannot afford it; his head and voice are much too valuable to us.”

Mr. Tope, in respectful convulsion, murmured that surely any gentleman would deem it a pleasure and an honour to have his neck broken in return for such a compliment from such a source.

“I will take it upon myself, sir,” Mr. Sapsea announced, “to answer for Mr. Jasper’s neck. I will tell Durdles to be careful of it. He will mind what I say. How is it at present endangered?” He cast the question abroad with a magnificent patronage, as if necks in general were an item he supervised.

“Only by my making a moonlight expedition with Durdles among the tombs, vaults, towers, and ruins,” Jasper returned. “You remember suggesting, when you brought us together, that, as a lover of the picturesque, it might be worth my while?”

“I remember!” said Mr. Sapsea. And, in that moment, he truly believed he did.

“Profiting by your hint,” Jasper pursued, “I have had some day-rambles with the extraordinary old fellow, and we are to make a moonlight hole-and-corner exploration to-night.”

“And here he is,” said the Dean.

Durdles came slouching up with his dinner-bundle in hand, as if he carried not food but some private lump of the day. The smell of him was of grit and lime and old stone that has been cut and wet and left to dry again; the sort of smell that fills the throat in a mason’s shed and makes you aware of your teeth. Seeing the Dean, he took off his hat and was slouching away with it under his arm when Mr. Sapsea stopped him.

“Mind you take care of my friend,” Mr. Sapsea commanded.

“What friend o’ yourn is dead?” Durdles asked. “No orders has come in for any friend o’ yourn.”

“I mean my live friend there.”

“O! him?” Durdles said. “He can take care of himself, can Mister Jarsper.”

“But do you take care of him too,” said Sapsea.

Durdles, feeling the command in the tone rather than any logic in the words, gave the Mayor a sour, deliberate survey from head to foot.

“With submission to his Reverence the Dean, if you’ll mind what concerns you, Mr. Sapsea, Durdles he’ll mind what concerns him.”

“You’re out of temper,” said Mr. Sapsea, winking to the company to observe how suavely he would manage him. “My friend concerns me, and Mr. Jasper is my friend. And you are my friend.”

“Don’t you get into a bad habit of boasting,” Durdles retorted, with a grave nod as if delivering a mason’s measurement. “It’ll grow upon you.”

“You are out of temper,” Mr. Sapsea repeated, reddening, yet still winking as though the redness were part of his method.

“I own to it,” Durdles returned. “I don’t like liberties.”

Mr. Sapsea winked a third time, as who should say, I think you will agree I have settled his business, and stalked out of the controversy.

Durdles gave the Dean good evening and added, setting on his hat again, “You’ll find me at home, Mister Jarsper, as agreed, when you want me; I’m a-going home to clean myself,” and slouched away.

This “cleaning himself” was one of his bargains with propriety. He never appeared cleaner—his hat, his boots, his coat always wearing the same perpetual crust of dust, as if Cloisterham’s stones had claimed him for kin—but the phrase served him like a ritual phrase serves a churchman: it marked the hour and excused the act.

The Dean withdrew to dinner; Mr. Tope to tea; Jasper to his piano. There, with no light but the fire’s, he sat chanting low choir-music, voice flowing like dark wine from a careful bottle, for two or three hours; until the town had grown still, the last doors had muttered on their hinges, and the moon was about to rise.

Then he closed the piano softly. He changed his coat for a pea-jacket with a substantial wicker-cased bottle in its largest pocket, set on a low-crowned, flap-brimmed hat, and went out as quietly as if sound itself were a witness he did not wish to summon. No outward reason required such stealth; yet he moved as though some inward thing crouched and listened for his own footfall.

At Durdles’s unfinished house—more a hole in the city wall than a dwelling—he saw light. He picked his way among gravestones and broken stone-lumber in the yard, where moonlight already touched edges sidewise, making names look newly cut and newly accusatory. Two great saws had been left sticking in their blocks; in the shadow of the sentry-boxes the sawyers’ tools might have been the grin and teeth of two skeleton journeymen from the Dance of Death, ready to set to work on the next pair destined for Cloisterham’s ledger. Likely enough, the men who owned the saws were at supper and thought no more of mortality than of tomorrow’s wage.

“Ho! Durdles!”

The light moved; Durdles appeared at the door with it. His notion of “cleaning” had plainly involved bottle, jug, and tumbler rather than brush or water; no other instruments were visible in the bare brick room with rafters overhead and no plastered ceiling. A sour spirit-smell—spirits and stale smoke and the faint bitter tang of lime dust—lay in the place like a second atmosphere.

“Are you ready?”

“I am ready, Mister Jarsper. Let the old ’uns come out if they dare, when we go among their tombs. My spirit is ready for ’em.”

“Do you mean animal spirits, or ardent?”

“The one’s the t’other,” Durdles answered. “And I mean ’em both.”

He took down a lantern from a hook, pocketed a match or two in case he should need to light it, and went out with Jasper, dinner-bundle and all.

It was an unaccountable expedition. Durdles prowled among graves and ruins as naturally as other men walked to market; the stones were his livelihood and his habit, and the dead were, to him, a set of tenants whose leases he understood. But that Jasper—cathedral musician, domestic guest, man of cultivated ear—should choose to pace the same places for “moonlight effects” in such company, and at such an hour, was another matter. The town’s usual nocturnal soundscape—the measured far-off murmur of the High Street, a cart-wheel complaining, a late voice, a dog’s halfhearted bark—thinned here into hush. Even the lamplighter’s ladder had ceased its clink. The Close had the acoustic quality of old cloth laid over furniture: it muffled.

“’Ware that there mound by the yard-gate, Mister Jarsper,” said Durdles.

“I see it. What is it?”

“Lime.”

Mr. Jasper stopped and waited for him to come up; Durdles lagged, as if the very word had slowed him.

“What you call quick-lime?”

“Ay!” Durdles said. “Quick enough to eat your boots. With a little handy stirring, quick enough to eat your bones.”

They went on, passing the red windows of the Travellers’ Twopenny, where some late drinkers’ laughter leaked out thinly and then was shut back in by glass. Emerging into clearer moonlight, they crossed the Monks’ Vineyard and came to Minor Canon Corner, much of which lay in shadow until the moon should climb higher.

A closing house-door struck their ears: that clean, domestic clap that sounds, in quiet precincts, like a verdict. Two men came out—Mr. Crisparkle and Neville. Jasper’s face, in the dimness, took on a strange, sudden smile. He laid the palm of his hand upon Durdles’s breast and stopped him where he stood.

At that end of the Corner the shadow was profound; and there was a low dwarf wall—breast-high—the last boundary of a garden that had been, and was now a thoroughfare. Jasper and Durdles would have turned it in another moment; but, halted so abruptly, stood behind it.

“Those two are only sauntering,” Jasper whispered. “They will go out into the moonlight soon. Let us keep quiet here, or they will detain us, or want to join us, or what not.”

Durdles nodded and fell to munching fragments from his bundle. There was something pathetic in the homeliness of it: meat and bread and perhaps a bit of cheese carried into the precinct of the dead, as if all hours must be seasoned by eating. In that crunching, one heard life insist on itself. Jasper folded his arms upon the top of the wall and rested his chin on them. He did not watch the Minor Canon at all. He watched Neville—watched him as though his eye lay on the trigger of a loaded rifle and he had him covered and was waiting for the wind. Something in Jasper’s face expressed destructive power so plainly that Durdles paused with an unmunched piece lodged in his cheek, staring.

Meanwhile Mr. Crisparkle and Neville walked to and fro, quietly talking. Their words did not carry in full, only broken by echoes and swallowed by the Corner’s hush, but Jasper caught his own name more than once, like a note struck and repeated.

“This is the first day of the week,” Mr. Crisparkle could be distinctly heard to observe as they turned back; “and the last day of the week is Christmas Eve.”

“You may be certain of me, sir,” Neville replied.

The echoes favoured those phrases and then betrayed them. Jasper caught “confidence,” shattered and pieced together by the stone. As they drew nearer, a fragment came clear: “Not deserved yet, but shall be, sir.” When they turned away again, Jasper heard his own name joined with Mr. Crisparkle’s words: “Remember that I said I answered for you confidently.” The rest became confused; Neville made some earnest action; and then Mr. Crisparkle looked up at the sky and pointed before him. They passed out into the moonlight at the far end and slowly disappeared.

Jasper did not move until they were gone. Then, abruptly, he turned to Durdles and burst into laughter—laughter that did not belong to the Corner’s silence and yet seemed bred by it. Durdles, with that suspended morsel still in his cheek, saw nothing to laugh at and stared. Jasper laid his face down on his arms to have the laugh out. Durdles, as if resigning himself to indigestion and to mysteries beyond masonry, bolted the morsel.

After dark there was almost no stir in these nooks. There was little enough even at noon; but at night the Close seemed to hold its breath. The High Street ran near, and its traffic was the town’s natural channel; yet between it and these precincts the Cathedral rose like a barrier that stopped not only feet but sound. Ask a hundred Cloisterham citizens at midday whether they believed in ghosts, and ninety-nine would say no; ask them at night whether they would take this shorter route or the longer round by shop-lamps and familiar voices, and ninety-nine would choose the longer. It was not local superstition, though a mysterious lady with a child in her arms and a rope at her neck had been seen flitting by witnesses as intangible as herself. It was something more bodily than belief: dust with breath in it shrinking from dust where breath had passed away; and, too, that half-admitted thought that if the dead ever did show themselves, these would be the likeliest surroundings. Even the ear seemed to share the caution. In the Close, every footstep sounded too loud, as if it might wake something.

When Jasper and Durdles paused before a small side door by which the latter had a key, and glanced round, the moonlit expanse was utterly deserted. It was as if the tide of life were stemmed by Jasper’s own gatehouse. One could hear the murmur of it beyond, but no wave passed the archway; Jasper’s lamp burned red behind its curtain like a lighthouse warning ships off.

They entered, locked themselves in, went down rugged steps, and were in the Crypt. The lantern was not needed: moonlight struck through groined windows bare of glass; the broken frames cast patterned bars on the ground like pale latticework. Heavy pillars supported the roof and bred black masses of shade, but between them ran lanes of light. Up and down these lanes they walked, Durdles discoursing of “the old ’uns” he yet counted on disinterring, slapping a wall in which he believed “a whole family on ’em” were stoned and earthed up, just as if he were on familiar visiting terms with the household. His usual taciturnity had been loosened by Jasper’s wicker bottle, which circulated freely—meaning its contents entered freely into Durdles’s circulation. Jasper himself only rinsed his mouth once and cast forth the rinsing, as if he would taste without swallowing, taking the scent and promise rather than the warmth.

They were to ascend the great Tower. On the steps that rose towards the Cathedral level, Durdles paused to gather breath. The stairs were very dark, but out of the darkness they could see those lanes of moonlight below, like strips of pale cloth laid in order. Durdles sat on a step. Jasper sat on another. The smell of spirit soon thickened; the bottle—somehow now in Durdles’s keeping—had plainly been opened. They could not see each other; yet in speaking they turned their faces as though eyes and mouths might meet in the dark.

“This is good stuff, Mister Jarsper!”

“It is very good stuff, I hope.—I bought it on purpose.”

“They don’t show, you see, the old ’uns don’t, Mister Jarsper!”

“It would be a more confused world than it is, if they could.”

“Well, it would lead towards a mixing of things,” Durdles conceded, as if the chief objection to spectres was that they muddled housekeeping. He pondered, then asked with a mason’s stubborn curiosity, “But do you think there may be Ghosts of other things, though not of men and women?”

“What things? Flower-beds and watering-pots? Horses and harness?”

“No. Sounds.”

“What sounds?”

“Cries.”

“What cries do you mean? Chairs to mend?”

“No. I mean screeches. Now I’ll tell you, Mr. Jarsper. Wait a bit till I put the bottle right.” The cork was evidently fussed with—out and in again. “There! Now it’s right! This time last year, only a few days later, I happened to have been doing what was correct by the season, in the way of giving it the welcome it had a right to expect, when them town-boys set on me at their worst. At length I gave ’em the slip, and turned in here. And here I fell asleep. And what woke me? The ghost of a cry. The ghost of one terrific shriek, which shriek was followed by the ghost of the howl of a dog: a long, dismal, woeful howl, such as a dog gives when a person’s dead. That was my last Christmas Eve.”

“What do you mean?” Jasper retorted, abrupt—almost fierce, as if a wrong note had been struck in his hearing.

“I mean that I made inquiries everywhere about, and that no living ears but mine heard either that cry or that howl. So I say they was both ghosts; though why they came to me, I’ve never made out.”

“I thought you were another kind of man,” Jasper said, with scorn that seemed aimed not only at Durdles but at the idea that sound might outlast sense.

“So I thought myself,” Durdles returned, composed. “And yet I was picked out for it.”

Jasper had risen suddenly when he demanded what Durdles meant; now he said, “Come; we shall freeze here; lead the way.”

Durdles got up, not very steadily, used his key again, and they emerged on the Cathedral level in a passage beside the chancel. Here the moonlight was so bright that the nearest stained-glass window threw its colours upon their faces—purple and yellow splashes like bruises and jaundice. Durdles, holding the door open for Jasper to follow as if he were letting him out of a grave, looked ghastly with the colour laid across him; yet he bore Jasper’s close scrutiny without consciousness. Jasper’s hands were busy at his pockets, seeking a key confided to him that would open an iron gate and admit them to the staircase of the great tower.

“That and the bottle are enough for you to carry,” Jasper said, passing the bottle to Durdles. “Hand your bundle to me; I am younger and longer-winded than you.”

Durdles hesitated between bundle and bottle as between duty and delight; but the bottle was by far the better company, and he kept it, consigning the dry weight to Jasper.

Then they went up the winding staircase of the great tower—turning and turning, shoulders and heads lowered to avoid the stair above or the rough stone pivot around which they twisted. Durdles lit the lantern by striking from the cold hard wall a spark of that hidden fire that lives in all things; and by that small star they clambered through cobwebs and dust. They passed through strange places: low-arched galleries where they could look down into the moonlit nave, and where, when Durdles waved his lantern, the dim carved angels’ heads on the corbels seemed to move and watch. Then into narrower, steeper staircases; the night-air began to blow upon them; a startled jackdaw or frightened rook chirped in the confined space, wings beat heavily against stone, and dust and straw rained on their heads as the bird forced past. At last, leaving their light behind a stair because the wind blew fresh up here, they looked down on Cloisterham spread fair in the moonlight: ruins and sanctuaries of the dead at the tower’s base; moss-softened red-tiled roofs and red-brick houses of the living beyond; and the river winding down from the mist on the horizon as though it rose from that whiteness, already heaving with a restless knowledge that its course ran seaward.

Again, what an unaccountable expedition. Jasper—still moving softly, as if even stone could hear—contemplated the scene, especially that stillest part of it which the Cathedral overshadowed. But he contemplated Durdles quite as curiously. Durdles, by times, felt the watchful eyes and shifted, uneasy; only by times, because he was growing drowsy.

As balloon-men lighten their load when they wish to rise, so Durdles had lightened the wicker bottle in coming up. Sleep caught him in snatches, surprising him on his legs and stopping his speech in the middle like a tool dropped. A mild calenture took him: he imagined the ground far below level with the tower, and would as willingly have walked out into air as along the stone. In such a state they began to come down. And as balloon-men make themselves heavier when they wish to descend, so Durdles charged himself with more liquid from the bottle to come down the better.

They reached the iron gate and locked it—not before Durdles had tumbled twice and once cut an eyebrow open—and descended into the crypt again, meaning to issue by the way they had entered. But returning among the lanes of moonlight between the pillars, Durdles grew so uncertain in foot and speech that he half dropped, half threw himself down by one of the heavy columns—scarcely less heavy than himself—and, in a thick, indistinct appeal, begged his companion for forty winks of a second each.

“If you will have it so, or must have it so,” Jasper replied, “I’ll not leave you here. Take them, while I walk to and fro.”
